title: Sell Mineral Rights in Illinois
metaTitle: Sell Gas Royalties in Illinois | Illinois Basin Owners
metaDescription: Illinois basin production is oil-dominant with limited gas. If you hold a small Illinois gas royalty, we'll give you an honest read and a written offer.
heroLead: the gas royalty desk will say this plainly before you read another word: Illinois is not a gas state, and if someone's telling you otherwise about your interest, get a second opinion.
intro: The Illinois basin, stretching across the southern third of the state into parts of Indiana and Kentucky, has been oil country for over a century, with waterflood and secondary recovery keeping thousands of shallow, mature wells producing long after their initial decline. Associated gas comes up with a lot of that oil, but the basin was never developed as a gas target the way the Fayetteville or Haynesville were, and most Illinois operators treat gas as a byproduct rather than the target. That distinction shapes almost every conversation we have with an Illinois owner about what their check actually represents.

That matters for how you should think about any royalty check tied to Illinois production. If gas shows up on your statement at all, it's very likely a small line item riding alongside a larger oil number, and in a lot of cases small-volume associated gas from marginal wells doesn't get metered and sold at all — it gets flared or used on lease rather than marketed.

sections.heading: What actually shows up on an Illinois statement
paragraphs: Most Illinois basin wells are old, shallow, and produce modest volumes by modern standards — this isn't a horizontal shale field, it's mostly vertical wells drilled decades ago that have been kept alive through waterflooding and workovers. Any gas revenue tends to be small and inconsistent month to month, more a rounding error on the statement than a driver of it. Waterflood economics also mean the oil side of the check can hold up longer than gas volumes would on their own, which is worth knowing before you assume the whole interest is fading fast.

If you're holding an interest specifically because you were told it's a gas play, pull your last few statements and add up the actual gas line versus the oil line before making any decisions. The numbers usually tell the real story faster than a conversation can. We've had owners come to us convinced they held a gas interest, only to find the gas line on their statement had been zero for years.

sections.heading: Who typically owns Illinois basin minerals
paragraphs: A lot of what we see is multi-generation family land in the southern counties — Wayne, Marion, Clay, and similar areas — where minerals were severed from surface ownership decades ago and have been passed down through wills and intestate succession since. Fractional interests are common, and courthouse records in some of these counties can be thin on recent conveyances even when the underlying production has kept paying reliably.

If you inherited a piece of land like this and have no real connection to the acreage, a mature low-volume interest is often more useful sold outright than held indefinitely for small, irregular checks. We see this a lot with out-of-state heirs who never expected to own Illinois mineral acreage in the first place and would rather have the cash than manage a distant, modest asset.

sections.heading: Being straight about value
paragraphs: We'll look at your actual production history, note honestly how much of it is gas versus oil, and price the interest against what it really is rather than what it sounds like it should be. A mostly-oil Illinois interest with a token gas component gets valued as an oil interest with a small bonus, not marketed as a gas asset it isn't.

If the honest answer is that your interest is small and declining with limited upside, we'd rather tell you that up front than waste your time with an inflated number that won't survive a real look at the production data. That honesty is also why owners tend to come back to us when a relative asks about selling their own piece of the same tract.

faqs.question: Is there real natural gas production in Illinois?
faqs.answer: Some, but it's a minor byproduct of oil-focused waterflood operations in the Illinois basin, not a targeted gas play. Volumes and revenue from gas are typically small compared to the oil.

faqs.question: Why doesn't your statement show any gas revenue?
faqs.answer: On a lot of marginal, low-volume Illinois wells, associated gas isn't metered or sold at all — it's flared or used on-site, which means it never generates royalty revenue in the first place.

faqs.question: Is a small fractional Illinois interest worth selling?
faqs.answer: Often, yes, particularly for heirs with no connection to the land. A small, mature interest with modest, declining checks can make more sense as a lump-sum sale than years of small payments.

faqs.question: Will you tell you honestly if your interest has limited value?
faqs.answer: Yes. We'd rather give you an accurate number based on your real production history than an inflated figure that falls apart once we look at the statements.

faqs.question: What documents should you gather before calling about an Illinois interest?
faqs.answer: Recent check stubs, a division order if you have one, and any old lease paperwork you can find. If you're missing most of that, we can still start with your county and legal description and track down the rest ourselves.
